subject: Culture
title: Lunar New Year Red Envelopes
description: One-minute skill: Lunar New Year Red Envelopes.

hook.text: During Lunar New Year, Chinese elders give children red envelopes stuffed with cash. The color wards off evil.

buildup.text: The tradition traces to a legend where coins tied with red string protected a child from a demon named Sui.

discovery.text: The amount matters: even numbers are lucky, but the number four is avoided because it sounds like 'death.'

twist.text: WeChat's digital red envelope feature sent 46 billion virtual envelopes in 2021. Tradition went cashless.

climax.text: Red envelopes flow upward too—employees give bosses envelopes as thanks, encoding workplace hierarchy.

punchline.text: Even cash gifts carry coded social messages.

quiz.question: Why is the number four avoided in red envelope amounts?

details.summary: Red envelopes (hongbao) filled with money are the centerpiece of Lunar New Year gift-giving in Chinese, Vietnamese, and other East Asian cultures. The red color wards off evil, and the enclosed money brings prosperity.
details.whyItMatters: Red envelopes bridge ancient tradition and digital innovation. Their evolution from physical to digital reveals how technology transforms cultural practices without destroying their meaning.
takeaways: Red envelopes contain money given during Lunar New Year celebrations
WeChat digital red envelopes process billions of transactions annually
The amount must avoid the number four (associated with death)

faq.question: What are the rules for red envelopes?
faq.answer: Give new, crisp bills (not old or wrinkled). Amounts should be even numbers (odd numbers are for funerals) and avoid the number four (sounds like 'death'). Numbers containing eight (prosperity) are ideal. Married adults give to children and unmarried young people. Accept with both hands.

faq.question: How did digital red envelopes transform the tradition?
faq.answer: WeChat launched digital red envelopes in 2014, and 8 billion were sent during Chinese New Year 2019. The feature added gamification — users can send random-amount envelopes where recipients compete to open them first.
